summary: Defines requirements for IPv6 nodes, so IPv6 works well and interoperates across many devices and deployments. It is Best Current Practice and obsoletes RFC 6434, and in turn RFC 4294.

eli5.summary: This is a checklist of things every device speaking the new internet addresses must be able to do.

subtitle: A single checklist of which IPv6 specifications every host and router should implement, and which are optional.

tldr.problem: IPv6 is spread over many specifications, and implementers of hosts, routers and small devices need to know which ones matter for interoperability.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC is an applicability statement. It walks through the layers of the stack and marks each referenced specification as MUST, SHOULD or MAY, without redefining the protocols.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 6434 and gives a minimal baseline for useful Internet service. Other profiles can add stricter rules for specific environments.

today: RFC 8504 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 220) published in January 2019. It obsoletes RFC 6434, and the metadata shows no later RFC obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: What the Document Is For
sections.content:
RFC 8504 defines common functionality required by both IPv6 hosts and routers. It borrows the definitions from RFC 8200: a node is a device that implements IPv6, a router is a node that forwards IPv6 packets not addressed to itself, and a host is any node that is not a router.

The document is an applicability statement. It collects requirements from other Standards Track documents in one place and avoids protocol detail. It does not update any individual protocol RFC.

The requirements are a minimal level needed for a device to provide useful Internet service. Other profiles may add stricter rules. The RFC gives the example that it does not mandate DHCP on all clients, but some deployments may require it. As an overriding principle, nodes should follow Jon Postel's Robustness Principle: be conservative in what you do, be liberal in what you accept from others.
sections.eli5: It is a checklist, not a rulebook for how things work inside. It tells makers of devices which IPv6 features to include so their gadgets get along with everyone else's.

sections.title: Reading the MUSTs and SHOULDs
sections.content:
The key words MUST, SHOULD and MAY carry their RFC 2119 and RFC 8174 meanings. Many specifications contain several independent pieces, and some are not mandatory, so a requirement can be smaller than a whole specification. Many specifications also define both client and server behaviour, while an implementation may only play one role.

At the lowest layer, an IPv6 node MUST support one or more IPv6 link-layer specifications. A conformant node may support IPv6 on some of its interfaces and not on others. The RFC lists link layers such as Ethernet, Frame Relay, IEEE 1394, Fibre Channel, IEEE 802.15.4, IEEE 802.16 and PPP for information only, and notes tunnelling such as Teredo.
sections.eli5: MUST means you cannot skip it, SHOULD means skip it only with a good reason, and MAY means it is up to you.

sections.title: The IP Layer: Packets, Fragments and Extension Headers
sections.content:
Support for RFC 8200 is a MUST. Every node MUST be able to send, receive and process Fragment headers, while forwarding MAY be supported. Nodes MUST NOT create overlapping fragments, and if a reassembled datagram contains an overlapping fragment, the whole datagram MUST be silently discarded. Nodes MUST NOT generate atomic fragments, and SHOULD avoid predictable Fragment Identification values.

Nodes MUST be able to process the extension headers, except Routing Header type 0, which was deprecated for security reasons and MUST be treated as an unrecognized routing type. The RFC discourages defining new extension headers unless an option in an existing one cannot do the job.

Because the only limit on extension headers is the MTU, long chains could be used for denial of service. A host MAY therefore limit them. Examples: limit consecutive PAD1 options to 7, limit a PADN option to less than 8 bytes, disallow unknown options (configurable, default is to accept them), and cap non-padding options, where the default SHOULD be 8.
sections.eli5: Think of a parcel with several wrapping layers. Every device must know how to unwrap them properly, but a careful device can refuse a parcel with a silly number of layers.

sections.title: Neighbor Discovery, MTU, ICMPv6 and Multicast
sections.content:
Neighbor Discovery (RFC 4861) MUST be supported. Hosts MUST support Router Discovery, Prefix Discovery and Neighbor Unreachability Detection, and MUST send Router Solicitations and receive Router Advertisements. All nodes MUST send and receive Neighbor Solicitation and Neighbor Advertisement messages, which Duplicate Address Detection needs. Nodes MUST NOT fragment Neighbor Discovery messages and MUST silently ignore them if fragmented. Hosts SHOULD process Redirects. Secure Neighbor Discovery (SEND) is optional, because of deployment complexity and very limited deployment experience.

Path MTU Discovery (RFC 8201) SHOULD be supported, though a minimal implementation may stay at packets of no more than 1280 octets. ICMPv6 Packet Too Big messages MUST NOT be filtered, since blocking them can cause black-hole connections. ICMPv6 (RFC 4443) MUST be supported.

Nodes that join multicast groups MUST support MLDv2 (RFC 3810), because one MLDv1-only node forces all others on the link into version 1 compatibility mode. Nodes SHOULD support ECN. IPv6 nodes MUST implement RFC 4191, and SHOULD implement the Type C host role.
sections.eli5: Neighbours on a street need to say hello and check who lives where. Devices do the same with Neighbor Discovery, and they must never block the polite note that says a package is too big for the road.

sections.title: Addresses and Configuration
sections.content:
The IPv6 Addressing Architecture (RFC 4291) MUST be supported. The current architecture is based on a 64-bit boundary for subnet prefixes. Hosts MUST support Stateless Address Autoconfiguration (SLAAC). It is RECOMMENDED to generate SLAAC addresses with the RFC 7217 procedure rather than embedding a MAC address in the interface identifier. All nodes MUST implement Duplicate Address Detection.

Privacy Extensions (RFC 4941) SHOULD be supported, and devices MUST let the end user enable or disable temporary addresses. All hosts SHOULD implement DHCPv6 address configuration. The rules of RFC 6724 for choosing among several addresses MUST be implemented.

For DNS, all nodes SHOULD implement a stub resolver with AAAA records, reverse lookup in ip6.arpa using PTR records, and EDNS(0) for packets larger than 512 octets. Implementations MUST support the DNS Router Advertisement option (RFC 8106), so SLAAC-only devices can find a resolver. A node that implements DHCP MUST implement its DNS options. There is no DHCPv6 gateway option, so default routers come from Router Advertisements. mDNS and DNS-SD SHOULD be supported where service discovery is useful.
sections.eli5: When you move into a new street, you need an address, a way to check nobody else has it, and the phone number of the directory service. These rules say how devices get all three.

sections.title: IPv4 Coexistence, Applications and Mobility
sections.content:
IPv6 nodes MAY support IPv4. If a node implements dual stack and tunnelling, RFC 4213 MUST be supported. Software that takes IPv6 addresses as text SHOULD support the representation recommended in RFC 5952. The RFC does not mandate any socket API, since the API does not affect behaviour on the wire, but it points to the basic and advanced IPv6 socket APIs.

On mobility, the RFC says Mobile IPv6 has seen only limited implementation and no significant deployment, partly because it assumed an IPv6-only environment. Mobile IPv6 and associated standards are therefore a MAY.
sections.eli5: Old and new road systems exist side by side. A device can use both, but if it does, it must follow the rules for crossing between them.

sections.title: Security: IPsec Is a SHOULD
sections.content:
IPv6 originally mandated IPsec. RFC 6434 relaxed this to a SHOULD for the IPsec architecture (RFC 4301), and this document keeps that. Nodes that implement it MUST implement ESP and MAY implement AH. The recommended automated key-management protocol is IKEv2, and manual keying is not recommended.

The RFC says no single security technology suits all cases, and IPsec is unlikely to displace TLS, SSH and others. Special-purpose or very constrained devices may reasonably use other approaches. Implementations MUST conform to the algorithm requirements of RFC 8221 and allow migration to new algorithms. Because most platforms enable IPv6 by default, networks that think of themselves as IPv4-only still face IPv6 security issues, and RFC 7123 gives guidance. The document itself does not directly affect Internet security beyond the individual protocols.
sections.eli5: A lock on every door sounds good, but a tiny garden shed does not need a bank vault. The rules say use strong locks where they fit and pick other protection where they do not.

sections.title: Routers, Constrained Devices and Changes
sections.content:
Routers MUST send Router Advertisements and process Router Solicitations. Forwarding nodes MUST conform to BCP 198 (RFC 7608). DHCP server function on routers is optional, but routers in complex networks SHOULD support relay agents. Management through SNMP, NETCONF and RESTCONF MAY be supported, with certain MIB and YANG modules as SHOULD where an agent exists.

For constrained devices, the requirements are RECOMMENDED for all nodes, but compromises may be needed. Interoperability must still be considered, since for instance supporting only MLDv1 affects other nodes on the link. Battery powered nodes SHOULD follow RFC 7772.

Appendix A lists changes from RFC 6434, including making MLDv2 and the DNS Router Advertisement option MUSTs, adding ECN and the extension-header protections, and removing Jumbograms and IPv6 over ATM because they are not deployed.
sections.eli5: Big routers and tiny battery sensors are both on the team. The checklist asks the small ones to do what they can, as long as they do not mess up the game for others.
